Switches dithering on or off, which hides banding in gradients. With Dither on, lighting, textures and fog of 3D drawing also get noise of less than half a step of the 8 bit buffer before they are rounded to it (and before blending), so a smooth gradient in an RGBA8 buffer is a fine pattern instead of bands. Only a buffer of 8 bits per color or less gets this noise: the 10 and 16 bit buffers of [Graphics3D](Graphics3D) depths 30 and 64 keep what the shader makes as it is, and the noise is added once, when the picture is turned into the 8 bits of the window. It uses the same moving noise (or the Bayer matrix, see [DitherMode](DitherMode)), costs a few operations per pixel, and colors that 8 bits can show exactly do not change. Blending is fixed-function with Dither 1, so what it makes is rounded again and a blend of a color over a gradient can still show bands. Besides that, the picture in the window gets temporal Interleaved Gradient Noise of up to half a step of the 8 bit output added when it is shown, so that the bands that rounding makes (for instance after SetGamma and UpdateGamma changed a gradient to values in between two steps) become a fine pattern that the eye averages out. The pattern moves from frame to frame (it repeats after 64 frames), which makes it average out over time as well; [DitherTemporal](DitherTemporal) keeps it in place instead. The noise is made on the GPU while the picture is shown, costs one pass over the screen, and does not change the buffers: ReadPixel and SaveBuffer see what was drawn (for the picture of the window; what 3D drawing made in a buffer of 8 bits or less is dithered when it is drawn, so ReadPixel sees that noise). A color that the picture can show exactly stays as it is.

Dither 2 is a BlitzLLVM extension that goes further: things that are drawn with a blend mode (alpha, multiply, add, or the texture blend modes that blend with what is there) are blended by their fragment shader instead of the fixed-function blender, which reads what the buffer holds at the pixel, mixes it as the blend mode says in floating point, adds the noise and only then rounds to 8 bits. That is how the result of a blend gets dithered, for instance a translucent fog sprite over a dark gradient. It takes the Vulkan extensions VK_KHR_dynamic_rendering_local_read and VK_EXT_rasterization_order_attachment_access, or else VK_EXT_fragment_shader_interlock (used with RGBA8 buffers, where the blending draws run in a pass of their own), which many current GPUs and drivers offer; [HWDither](HWDither) says whether the one in use does. With the depths 16, 15 and 12 of [Graphics3D](Graphics3D) the noise of 3D drawing is one step of the 5, 6 or 4 bits that the buffer has, and with the depth 8 the shader adds noise of one step of the palette ([GraphicsPalette](GraphicsPalette)) after lighting and fog, before the nearest color is picked (Dither 2 blends first, so the blend is in palette colors). Dither 2 only blends in the shader when the target has 8 bits per color (alpha does not count), which is where the noise is needed: into the 10 and 16 bit buffers of [Graphics3D](Graphics3D) depths 30 and 64 the fixed-function blender is used, as with Dither 1. Where the GPU can not do it, or while [AntiAlias](AntiAlias) is on (smoothing needs the finished picture of the camera), Dither 2 does exactly what Dither 1 does. Blending in the shader costs a little more per blended pixel than the fixed-function blender, and the drawing of things that are not blended, or with Dither 0 or 1, does not use it.
@param enable  0 (False) not to dither, 1 (True) to dither, and 2 to dither what blending makes as well, see HWDither. It is off by default, and unlike in the original it does not matter which color depth was asked for.
